---
title: "The level meter"
description: Read the two-row meter in the timeline bar to see how loud the mix is while it plays, and whether it reaches full scale.
---

import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

The level meter shows how high the mix you're hearing sits while the timeline plays, and warns you when a sample reaches full scale.

<AtAGlance where="The timeline bar, just left of the zoom controls" />

## What it shows

The meter shows what you hear: each clip's volume, fades, ducking, mute and solo, and the compressor and other effects. Press play and it moves. There's nothing to turn on.

It has two rows, one per channel, with the left channel on top. A mono track shows in both rows, and a track with more than two channels shows only its first two.

At normal speed it measures the mix itself, so two tracks playing the same sound read as one louder sound, and a sound and its inverse read as silence. At any other speed it adds up each track's level instead. That can read a little higher than the mix, and it can light the clip cell when the mix itself wouldn't reach full scale.

## Read the meter

Each row runs from −60 dB on the left to 0 dB on the right. The scale is even in dB, so the middle of a row is −30 dB. It has no tick marks.

| Part | What it tells you |
| --- | --- |
| **Solid bar** | The average (RMS) level. It rises at once and falls at 24 dB a second. |
| **Lighter wash** behind the bar | The instantaneous peak. It rises and falls the same way, and it's never shorter than the bar. |
| **Peak-hold mark** | The highest recent level. It stays for about 1.2 seconds, then falls at 12 dB a second. |
| **Clip cell** at the right end of each row | Lights for 2 seconds whenever a sample in that row reaches full scale. |

A level above 0 dB fills the row and goes no further, so the clip cell is what tells you the mix went over.

## When playback stops

The bars fall back to the floor. The peak-hold mark stops waiting and falls with them, and a lit clip cell stays lit for the rest of its 2 seconds. The whole meter is at rest within about 3 seconds.

## Good to know

- The meter shows peaks and average level, not loudness. For LUFS and true peak, use [the Loudness Meter](/audio/loudness-meter/).
- It shows the preview's mix. An export also goes through a master limiter, so what an export measures can differ. See [Export loudness](/export/loudness/).
- There's one meter for the whole app. With two projects open, the meter in both windows follows the one that's playing, and stopping one project doesn't blank the meter while the other plays on.
- In a narrow window the meter gets smaller, and below 40 points wide it isn't drawn at all.
- The recorder panel has its own meter for the microphone. See [The recorder panel](/recording/recorder-panel/).

## Related

- [The Loudness Meter](/audio/loudness-meter/)
- [Mute and solo tracks](/audio/mute-and-solo/)
- [Limiter](/audio/limiter/)
- [Play, pause and shuttle](/timeline/playback/)

---
title: "The Loudness Meter"
description: Show a live column beside the preview that measures your mix in LUFS and true peak while it plays at normal speed.
---

import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
import Shot from '@components/Shot.astro';

The Loudness Meter tells you how loud your mix really is, measured the way the loudness standards EBU R 128 and ITU-R BS.1770 measure it, while the preview plays at normal speed.

<AtAGlance
  menu="View ▸ Loudness Meter"
  keys="⌃⌘L"
  where="A column at the right of the preview, left of the scopes"
/>

<Shot
  name="04c-editor-loudness.preview"
  alt="The preview with the Loudness column at its right edge, before anything has played. The column has a Reset arrow at the top, M and S bars on a scale from 0 to −48 with a thin blue line across them just above −18, then Momentary, Short-term, Integrated and True peak max, each reading a dash, and a note saying this is the mix as the preview plays it, before the export's loudness and master limiter."
/>

## Show the meter

Choose **View ▸ Loudness Meter** or press <kbd>⌃⌘L</kbd>. The same command hides it, and the menu item has a tick while the column is showing. The column is 132 points wide and as tall as the preview pane, and the picture makes room for it.

Then play the timeline at normal speed. The figures start at "—" and fill in as Frame Job measures.

## What it measures

The meter measures the mix you hear, including every clip's and track's sound, and it follows each track's own position, so a gap between clips doesn't disturb it. It only reads what plays. It never changes the project or an export.

Measuring carries on while the column is hidden. If you show it partway through a pass, the figures already include what has played.

A mono track counts in both channels. A track with more than two channels counts by its first two.

## The four figures

| Figure | What it measures |
| --- | --- |
| **Momentary** | The last 0.4 seconds. |
| **Short-term** | The last 3 seconds. |
| **Integrated** | Everything measured since the last reset, with quiet passages left out as the standard says. |
| **True peak max** | The highest true peak since the last reset. It turns coral above −1 dBTP. |

Figures have one decimal place, such as `−18.4 LUFS` or `−0.6 dBTP`.

| You see | It means |
| --- | --- |
| "—" | There's no figure yet. Momentary needs 0.4 seconds of measuring and Short-term needs 3. Integrated stays at "—" until something loud enough to count has played, so it stays there through digital silence. |
| "−∞" | Digital silence. |

## The M and S bars

The two bars show Momentary (**M**) and Short-term (**S**) on a scale from −48 to 0 LUFS, with a tick every 6 LU. A bar is empty while its figure is "—", and during digital silence.

## The target line

A thin line in the accent colour crosses both bars at the target in the [Normalize](/audio/normalize/) row, which is −16 LUFS unless you've changed it. It shows you where the mix sits against the level Normalize aims for.

The line moves as soon as you change the target, even while the preview is paused. The target can go as low as −50 LUFS, and anything below −48 draws at the bottom of the scale. The line stays at the stored target when Normalize is in Peak mode.

## Start measuring again

Click the **Reset** button, the ↺ at the top of the column. All four figures go back to "—" and the next sound starts a new measurement.

The meter also starts again by itself when you jump somewhere else, such as a seek, the loop going round, or playing from another place. It does the same if Frame Job can't keep up with the audio, because a measurement with a hole in it would be wrong.

These don't restart it:

- Pausing and playing on. Nothing is counted twice.
- An edit.
- A gap between clips.
- Holding a menu open.
- Stepping back by less than a second.

When playback stops, the figures stay where they were.

## Measuring only at normal speed

The meter measures at ×1 only. At any other speed, such as while you [shuttle](/timeline/playback/):

- Momentary and Short-term show "—" and their bars go empty.
- The note reads "Measured only at normal speed."
- Integrated and True peak max keep their values.

When you stop, Momentary and Short-term go back to their last normal-speed values.

## The note under the figures

The note says what's being measured, and when to take the figures with care.

| The note says | When |
| --- | --- |
| "The mix as the preview plays it, before the export's loudness and master limiter." | Usually. |
| "The mix as the preview plays it, with track compressors and limiters approximate, before the export's loudness and master limiter." | While any track has a [compressor or limiter](/audio/track-dynamics/). They're approximate in the preview and exact in an export. |
| "Measured only at normal speed." | While playing at any other speed. |

An export with a loudness target changes the level after this point, and the master limiter holds its peaks under the ceiling, so the export's own report can differ from what you see here. See [Export loudness](/export/loudness/).

## Good to know

- The meter belongs to its window. A new window starts with the column off and the meter empty.
- Nothing is saved. Closing the window ends the measurement, and the column is off the next time you open the project.

## With an agent

No agent tool shows this meter or reads it. An agent reads loudness from an export's report instead. See [Tools: export](/mcp/tools-export/).

## Related

- [The level meter](/audio/level-meter/)
- [Normalize](/audio/normalize/)
- [Export loudness](/export/loudness/)
- [Track compressor and limiter](/audio/track-dynamics/)

---
title: "Synchronize Audio"
description: Line up a camera and a separate recorder, or any clips of the same moment, by matching their sound.
---

import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

Synchronize Audio lines up two or more clips by their sound. The usual case is a camera clip and a separate audio recorder that captured the same moment. It finds where the sound matches, moves the clips into place and corrects any clock drift, all as one undo step.

<AtAGlance
  menu="Clip ▸ Synchronize Audio"
  tools="sync_audio"
  needs="Nothing. The matching and the voice detection run on your Mac, with no key and no upload."
/>

## Line up clips

<Steps>

1. Put each clip on its own track. They don't need to be close to each other.

2. If the recorder holds several similar stretches, trim it roughly around the camera's sound, so it [matches the right one](#matching-by-sound).

3. Select the clips.

4. Choose **Clip ▸ Synchronize Audio**. It has no keyboard shortcut.

5. Wait for the [Synchronizing Audio sheet](#the-synchronizing-audio-sheet) to finish.

</Steps>

One clip, the [anchor](#the-anchor), stays where it is. Every other clip slides along its own track until its sound plays at the same moment as the anchor's. The whole command is one undo step, named **Synchronize Audio**.

If Frame Job is sure of the match, it's applied straight away. If it isn't, Frame Job [asks you first](/audio/weak-sync-matches/).

It's all or nothing. If any clip can't be matched, nothing moves, and [the reasons are listed](#when-it-wont-run).

## Which clips it takes

**Clip ▸ Synchronize Audio** is available when at least two selected clips can play sound and aren't [nests](/editing/nests/).

Anything else in the selection is left out without a message: a nest, a still, a title, a file with no audio track, a clip with its audio switched off. To line up clips inside a nest, open it with <kbd>⌘↓</kbd> and select them there.

## The anchor

Frame Job picks the anchor this way:

1. Among the selected clips that have a picture, the one that starts earliest. If none has a picture, all of them are considered.
2. If two start at the same time, the one on the rearmost track.
3. If they're still tied, the one created first.

So a camera clip stays put and the recorder moves to it. The anchor is never moved or trimmed, and its speed doesn't change.

## Matching by sound

Each file's sound is analysed once, after it's imported, into a form that isn't thrown off by differences in gain, microphone or room. Frame Job compares the files, not the clips, so a clip's volume and effects make no difference.

- **Speech comes first.** When both clips hold at least 2 seconds of speech, as judged by the on-device voice model, only the speech is compared. Otherwise all the sound is.
- **The trimmed parts come first.** Frame Job looks within the parts each clip is trimmed to, when both are at least 2 seconds long. It searches the whole files only if that finds no usable match and at least one clip is trimmed.

:::tip
A recording with two similar stretches can match the wrong one. Trimming the recorder roughly around the camera's sound tells Frame Job which one you mean.
:::

## The waveform check

Sounding alike isn't enough, because two takes of the same words can look like a match. So a match is used only if the two waveforms also line up there, as a clear peak within 48 ms. Frame Job checks up to 30 seconds of the overlap, where the sound agrees most, in the speech band of 300 to 3,400 Hz.

The same check fine-tunes the offset to less than a frame.

## Moves land on whole frames

Clips move by a whole number of frames at the project's frame rate, so up to half a frame of constant offset can remain. At 30 fps that's about 17 ms.

## The head trim

If a clip would have to start before 0:00 to line up, it loses that much from its start instead, and starts at 0:00 in sync. Frame Job trims only what it has to. It won't do this if less than a frame of the clip would be left.

## Drift correction

Two devices' clocks never run at quite the same rate, so a recorder slowly falls out of sync over a long take. When the clips overlap for at least 60 seconds, Frame Job measures that drift along the overlap and corrects it by playing the moved clip at a slightly different speed, at most 0.2 % from ×1.

The correction is part of the same undo step. There's no drift figure to read. What changes is the clip's speed, which shows in the [Speed section](/speed/speed-section/), for example ×1.0004, with **Keep pitch** turned off. The clip gets very slightly longer or shorter to match.

Drift is left alone when:

- it's under 5 ms across the overlap
- it's too small to tell from no drift, meaning under three times its own uncertainty
- correcting it would take more than 0.2 % from ×1
- too little of the overlap matches to measure it

:::note
The correction is a plain resample, so the pitch moves very slightly with the speed. Like any clip with Keep pitch off at a speed other than ×1, the clip's sound is [rendered in the background](/speed/keep-pitch/#tape-pitch-is-rendered-in-the-background). It's briefly silent in the preview after the correction, and again after each trim, split or speed change. An export waits for it.
:::

## The Synchronizing Audio sheet

Matching runs in the background behind a **Synchronizing Audio** sheet, with a progress bar and the line "Matching the sound of N clips…". Nothing moves until a match is found.

**Cancel** or <kbd>Esc</kbd> closes the sheet and leaves everything as it was.

If the project changes while the matching runs, for example because an agent edits it, nothing is applied. Frame Job beeps and the inspector says to choose Synchronize Audio again.

## When it won't run

Frame Job beeps and lists every reason in [the strip at the foot of the inspector](/getting-started/refused-edits/#the-refusal-strip), naming each clip by its number. The strip shows three lines, so hover over it to read a long one.

It checks each clip first, and won't start matching until they all pass. A clip can't be lined up when it:

- plays no sound in the timeline
- is still being analysed. Its sound or speech analysis hasn't finished, so try again in a moment.
- comes from a file with under 2 seconds of sound
- plays more than 0.2 % away from ×1. Set it back to ×1 first.
- plays at a rate other than its speed setting
- plays [reversed](/speed/reverse/)
- [ramps its speed](/speed/speed-ramps/), because a speed action changes its rate over its length

The rest come up during the matching:

- Two of the clips are on one track. Each needs its own.
- A clip has no sound to line up by, because its analysis found no sound at all.
- Nothing matches. See [When nothing matches](/audio/weak-sync-matches/#when-nothing-matches).
- A clip matches the anchor's sound but the waveforms don't line up there, for example two takes of the same words. They aren't one recording.
- A clip matches the anchor's sound but the two share under 2 seconds of waveform there, too little to confirm it's one recording.
- A clip would lose so much of its head that less than a frame is left.
- A clip would never play at the same time as the anchor once lined up. Extend its trim, or the anchor's.
- A clip would overlap another clip on its own track after the move. Move that clip out of the way, or put this one on a free track.

## Good to know

If the clips are already in sync, nothing changes and Frame Job beeps. Choosing the command a second time on the same clips does this.

## With an agent

`sync_audio` does the same thing, with two differences. An agent can name the anchor, and it's told by name when it passes a nest or a clip that plays no sound, where the menu leaves those out. It also reports each clip's offset, confidence and drift, which the menu doesn't show. See [Tools: audio](/mcp/tools-audio/).

## Related

- [Confident and weak matches](/audio/weak-sync-matches/)
- [Keep pitch](/speed/keep-pitch/)
- [When an edit is refused](/getting-started/refused-edits/)
- [Nests](/editing/nests/)

---
title: "Confident and weak matches"
description: How Synchronize Audio grades a match, what the Weak match sheet asks you, and what to do when nothing matches.
---

import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

[Synchronize Audio](/audio/synchronize-audio/) grades every match it finds. A confident match is applied straight away, a weak one is asked about first, and anything less moves nothing.

<AtAGlance menu="Clip ▸ Synchronize Audio" tools="sync_audio" />

Each possible offset gets a **confidence**: a score for how far it stands out from every other offset Frame Job tried. A high score means one offset is clearly right. Frame Job keeps up to four candidates, each about a second or more from the others.

Either grade must also pass [the waveform check](/audio/synchronize-audio/#the-waveform-check). A match that fails it isn't used, however high its confidence.

## Confident matches

A match is confident when its best candidate has a confidence of at least 10, and is at least 1.5 above the next candidate. A confident match is applied straight away.

## The Weak match sheet

A match is weak when no candidate is confident, but the best one within about 3 seconds of where the clip already sits has a confidence of at least 4. A weak match might be unrelated sound, so it's never applied without asking. A **Weak match** sheet appears:

> Weak match: move “record.aifc” 0.80 s earlier (trimming 0.80 s off its head)?

A clip that doesn't need to move, only to have its drift corrected, is asked about this way:

> Weak match: play “record.aifc” at ×1.0004, correcting its drift?

When several clips are weak, one sheet lists them all, separated by semicolons.

Under the question, the sheet gives the anchor's name, each match's confidence and the rule it fell short of.

| Choose | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| **Apply** (the default) | Makes all the changes as one undo step, including those for any clips that matched confidently. |
| **Cancel** or <kbd>Esc</kbd> | Leaves everything as it is, including clips that matched confidently. |

If the project changed while the sheet was up, **Apply** moves nothing. Frame Job beeps and the inspector says to choose Synchronize Audio again.

A weak match that wouldn't change anything isn't asked about.

## When nothing matches

If no candidate is confident or weak, nothing moves. [The strip at the foot of the inspector](/getting-started/refused-edits/#the-refusal-strip) names the offsets Frame Job did find and their confidences, for example:

> no matching sound found between clip 1 and clip 2: in the played windows, moving clip 2 by +0.77 s (confidence 4.31) or −12.40 s (3.90)

"The played windows" are the parts each clip is trimmed to, and "the whole files" are listed too when those were searched. A plus sign means later and a minus sign means earlier. Hover over the strip to read the whole message.

To try again:

<Steps>

1. Pick the offset that looks right. You might know roughly where the clip belongs, or one figure may be well ahead of the others.

2. Move the clip by about that much, so it sits within 3 seconds of the match.

3. Choose **Clip ▸ Synchronize Audio** again. A candidate near the clip with a confidence of at least 4 now comes up as a weak match.

</Steps>

If the message ends "too little room to compare their sound", Frame Job found no candidates at all. Check that both clips have enough sound to compare, and try longer trims.

## Good to know

The whole files are searched only when the trimmed parts give neither a confident nor a weak match. A weak match in the trimmed parts ends the search, so if you cancel it, widen or narrow the trims before trying again.

## With an agent

An agent gets no sheet. A weak match moves nothing and the agent is told the move it would make, so it should ask you. It applies the match only once you've agreed. See [Tools: audio](/mcp/tools-audio/).

## Related

- [Synchronize Audio](/audio/synchronize-audio/)
- [When an edit is refused](/getting-started/refused-edits/)

## The refusal strip

> Refused: track 3 is locked, so the gap on it cannot be closed

The strip shows up to three lines. Rest the pointer on it to read the whole sentence.

It stays until you click it or the project changes, which means an edit, an undo or redo, or going into or out of a nest. Moving the playhead or changing the selection doesn't clear it, so you can look around while you work out what to do.

The sentence is exact rather than friendly. It can name clips and tracks by Frame Job's own numbers, which aren't their positions on the timeline, and give lengths in the timeline's smallest units rather than in seconds.

Each feature's page lists what can stop it, and [Troubleshooting](/reference/troubleshooting/) gathers them in one place.

A typed Start, Length or end value on an action shows the strip too. Dragging an action's band never does. See [Move, resize or remove an action](/motion/change-an-action/).

## A drop that springs back

3:Frame Job mixes sound from every clip that has it: a camera clip, an audio-only file, a microphone recording or a nest. Each clip has its own level, fades, ducking, voice isolation, a voice effect, channel choice, EQ, hum removal, noise reduction, gate, leveller, de-esser, compressor, pan and mono fold, and a true-peak limiter, and each track can be muted or soloed and has its own volume, pan, compressor and limiter. Four commands do the measuring for you. Normalize sets a clip's level from its loudness (or its loudest moment), Enhance Voice sets a voice recording up for speech from its own measurements, Match Audio gives clips another clip's loudness and tone, and Synchronize Audio lines up a camera and a separate recorder by their sound. The preview and the export use the same mix, so what you hear while editing is what gets written, except that every export also holds its peaks under −1 dBTP with a master limiter the preview doesn't have, and a track's compressor and limiter are exact in an export but approximate in the preview (see [Track compressor and limiter](#track-compressor-and-limiter)).
137:*Agents:* `enhance_voice` (`clips`; optional `target_lufs` from −50 to −5, default −16). Each row of `enhanced` gives the measurements (`measured_lufs`, `true_peak_dbtp`, `speech_seconds`, `floor_lufs`, `floor_gap_db`, `pause_peak_dbfs`, `sibilance_share`, `speech_range_lu`: null with under 3 s of speech), `set` (exactly the `set_audio` keys written), `reasons` (one sentence per rule), `volume`, `processed_lufs`, `renders`, `result_lufs` and `result_true_peak_dbtp` as the last render measured them, and `limited_by`. Skips are under `skipped`. A second call answers "Enhance Voice made no change".
154:*Agents:* `match_audio` (`reference`, `clips`; optional `loudness` and `eq`, both default true, refused when both are false). The answer gives `reference` (`clip`, `media`, `lufs`, `speech_seconds`), `target_lufs` (null with loudness off), and a row per clip under `matched`: `set` (exactly the `set_audio` keys written), `eq` and `eq_fit_rms_db` (how far the fitted EQ is from the measured difference), `volume`, `measured_lufs`, `processed_lufs`, `result_lufs`, `result_true_peak_dbtp`, `limited_by` and `renders`. Skips are under `skipped`. A second call answers "Match Audio made no change".
207:With **Clip Length**, ducking follows the clip's length on the timeline, not whether anyone is talking. The other audio stays lowered for the whole length of the ducking clip, through pauses, and comes back up only after the clip ends. You can therefore see exactly when ducking applies by looking at the timeline. If the attack is longer than the clip, the level never fully reaches Level, and the release starts from wherever it got to.
571:- **Approximate in the preview.** The preview plays a track's sound in more than one piece where its clips overlap (a crossfade, or a nest's tracks), and it runs the compressor and limiter on each piece separately, so the pieces can add up past a track limiter's ceiling while editing. Measured on two clips at −1 dBFS crossfading under a limiter at −6 dBTP, the preview's true peak was 5.2 dB over the ceiling; the export held it. The Loudness Meter says "approximate" while any track has a compressor or limiter.
572:- **What hears them.** The preview, the level meter and the Loudness Meter (approximately), and every export. Normalize, the Loudness read-out, Enhance Voice and Match Audio work on the clip itself, before the track, and don't.
616:The figures are the mix as the preview plays it, before the export's loudness setting and its master limiter, and the column says so. While any track has a compressor or limiter, it says they are approximate (see [Track compressor and limiter](#track-compressor-and-limiter)). An export with a loudness target changes the level after this point, and the master limiter holds its peaks under the ceiling, so its report can differ. The column is per window and turns off when you close the window.
709:- A track's compressor and limiter are approximate in the preview wherever its clips overlap (a crossfade, a nest's tracks); see [Track compressor and limiter](#track-compressor-and-limiter). A nest's own tracks have none, and scrubbing doesn't hear them.
720:- Attach Audio needs the picture and its sound to cover exactly the same time. Undo a J-cut or L-cut, or trim the two to match, before attaching.
